High on Ink

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A “paperless” Joburg is hoarding over R100 million in ink, R40 million of which can’t be used —exposing chaotic procurement, mountains of dead stock, and a supplier address that leads to a bou

Unique Selling Point:
We went undercover to the smit street stores to see the chaos. We have really great footage, and have a compelling story that will illustrate what a mess the asset management system is. In short: it says Joburg talks “modern, paperless city,” but runs on procure-first, plan-later. Transparency gap: basic spend and contracts aren’t clearly published or explained. Control failure: stock counts, write-offs, and auctions aren’t working; SAP/asset data isn’t driving decisions.
No standardisation: departments/IT change printers without checking stores → waste by design. Misaligned incentives: outsourced printing + leased printers (toner included) while buying separate cartridges anyway. Service impact: money that should fix pipes, power and roads is frozen on shelves. Accountability vacuum: everyone’s “aware,” nobody owns it. Bottom line: not just wastage—a governance problem that bleeds budgets and trust.

Summary:
ROUGH SCRIPT:OPENING ACT – A city that’s high on ink

Presenter VO: It was a slow Wednesday morning… one of our Carte Blanche producers drew the short straw: the July City of Johannesburg Council meeting. As expected —SOUNDUP: “Item 43” drier than a Joburg winter lawn.

UPSOUND – Neuren: video of him at council
“For a first-class African city, we should be doing better…”

Presenter VO: And then, during one of Councillor Neuren Pietersen’s trademark report-backs from an oversight visit to the City’s storerooms… something actually piqued her interest.

Cut to Council Audio (UPSOUND): Neuren Pietersen: “To date, the City is not privy to the detail of any contracts, which we are expected to note here today. We still don’t know how much we pay for a bottle of water, a pen, a ream of paper — or why we have R100 million worth of ink cartridges in stock that the City no longer uses!”

Presenter VO: That’s the kind of line that makes journalists bolt upright—faster than dodging a Joburg pothole. This was a story, with the councillor providing the punchlines.

Neuren in council: “To date, this councillor—yours truly—has never received an ink cartridge for my own HP DeskJet… something that’s meant to be included as part of a councillor’s tools of trade. I hope the Auditor-General is listening…”

Presenter VO: Well, she’s not the Auditor-General—but she does WhatsApp the councillor. He sends photos from his oversight visit: floor-to-ceiling cartridges.

INTV: Neuren: Turns out, at Smit Street Stores—one of the City’s storerooms—there are millions of rands’ worth of “dead stock”: expired cartridges, or cartridges for printers the City no longer uses.

Presenter link: The city says it wants to go paperless, council has already gone that route, so how can they justify spending that amount on printer cartridges? This is like squid games, only instead of dead people, its dead stock.

VO: At a time when the City is scratching around for money to fix potholes, keep the lights on, and even contemplating selling off public assets like our public parks— why are we spending a fortune on ink cartridges?


ACT 1: Why Ink?

Presenter VO: Neuren is a character — hard to miss in that Panama hat. His turf is Ward 118, from Linksfield to Cleveland — basically Joburg’s welcome mat as you roll in from the airport.

Montage (cutaways):
Uncut grass. Buckled pavements. A broken sever system.
UPSOUND – Neuren: “This has been waiting nine months to be fixed because Joburg didn’t have money for material.”
Cutaway: Substation has no security
UPSOUND – Neuren: “The substation has lots of theft and vandalism because there’s no security.”

Presenter VO: All of that is easy to see. But when he joined the finance committee, he spotted something you can’t see from the roadside. Of the City’s four consumables warehouses: Three were sitting at a few million each…but one then one was clocking over R100 million.

Presenter link [outside the warehouse]: That warehouse is here on Smit Street: Turns out it isn’t hoarding gold; but stationery—mostly ink cartridges. A one-hundred million rand ink-vestment?

Neuren: We spend R10 million on stationery per quarter—my guesstimate: R3 million on paper, R6 million on ink, minimum. It’s stockpiled in that warehouse.

VO: It’s hard to be accurate when the city is not transparent – for the last decade no tenders have been posted online for the public, no number breakdowns are given to council – it seems it’s a state secret…

Neuren: For example: we spent R10 million on paper products like toilet paper… but there’s no breakdown and we don’t know where the papers going, and we don’t know how much is used or left over…
and council has gone paperless, but the numbers for ink and paper – weirdly haven’t gone down?

VO: Exact figures? Hard to come by when the City treats numbers like a state secret—no tenders posted online for years, no line-item breakdowns to Council. Transparency is one item in the City perpetually out of stock.

UPSOUND – Neuren: “For example: we spent R10 million on paper products—like toilet paper—but there’s no breakdown. We don’t know where it’s going, how much is used, or what’s left over. And Council has gone ‘paperless’, yet the ink and paper numbers haven’t dropped?”

VO: Also—much of the City’s paperwork is outsourced. In our July story on Joburg parks, officials said most documents like tenders are prepared externally — and often printed off-site.

SOUNDUP from previous story: (date it)
Mac: Who writes these tender documents?”
Tshabalala: “We compile a list of what needs to be done and we appoint service providers.”

VO: And many departments don’t buy printers at all—they lease them: meaning toner is vendor-supplied.

Neuren: I’ve checked departments—Revenue, Health, Road Traffic Management Centre—trying to find City-owned printers that actually need cartridges… I’m still looking. On my oversight visit I was told the majority of cartridges go to the JMPD.

VO: But Whatsapps from a city insider says most of the JMPDs printers are leased.

SHOW WHATSAPPS: [The printers] are all on a rental lease… when the ink is closer to being finished, the lease company is contacted.

VO: So… if much of the printing is outsourced, and the leased printers come with their own toner… where is all this ink going?



ACT 2: The undercover

VO: Time to see for ourselves. We head to Smit Street Stores — undercover — with councillors Neuren Pietersen and David Foley, a ward councillor from Fourways, to illustrate the problem.

We’re walked through by an employee reporting back to the councillors — unaware we’re filming.

Downstairs, first stop: a room stacked wall-to-wall with thousands of expired printer cartridges.

[41. 25 all expired stock]
41.31 all of these are expired
S: so those lexmarks are expired?
Yes. These ones are expired. over 10 years old
S: 10 years? and you say it's over 2 million stock in here?
Employee: yes 2.7 million worth of expired stock.

VO: Ink economics aren’t sexy—until you’re staring at millions of rands of it - R2.7 million parked just in that corner.

[Video pan of expired stock 41.51]

VO: Roughly twenty million rands worth of stock is expired. So why is it sitting there instead of written off and auctioned?

Neuren: The City did write off a fraction—about 0.3%. Clipboards and notepads. The cartridges? They could go on auction, but there hasn’t been one this year. And no one wants to take responsibility.

VO: The employee gives us a clue why the cartridges haven’t been written off.

Undercover video: 1:00:50 Councillor: I don't understand why they why they're not bringing that up to the fore, why are they so resistant to say okay we've made a mistake, write it off, move on.
Employee: when you know that you have blundered, you will not stand up!

VO: In other words, it’s the usual story… no one wants to raise a hand and own the mistake. [pause]

Here’s the irony: councillors are entitled to one printer cartridge per quarter. And Neuren’s model is sitting right there.. But he still can’t even get one…as this city employee tells him…

CALL WITH NEUREN and PRESENTER: Karabo…

VO: But a bigger problem reveals itself as we wind through the two-storey warehouse. Shelves of “dead” stock: ink for printers the City no longer uses.

Undercover video: Visual: 59.28 – 59.50 [WALKING ALONG SHELVES SEEING DEAD STOCK]
Employee: all these cartridges are dead
Sasha: Canon, HP, Brother… OKI, Lexmark.

VO: Much of it is perfectly usable— Here’s a fact you didn’t ask for: what does R1 million in printer cartridges look like?

Undercover video: Visual: 46:00 WE SEE BOXES OF CARTRIDGES IN CORNER JUST SITTING THERE, NO LONGER BEING USED.
Upsound: 46.20 Sasha: and so wait so this is about a million rand here, but then I just wanna understand now, the amount of um…, that might not move again, so then what do you do with it?
Employee: it might not move again, take a picture and save it, it might not move again, a million rand stuck, standing there.

VO: And another million rand here — A monument to the City’s “procure first, plan later” mindset.

Undercover video: [47.20 /53.08 see the boxes without him]
47.20 Eployee: This was the old cartridge that JMPD was using, another million.
Ccouncillor: and how long has it been standing here?
Employee: it's almost a year now okay

Neuren intv:
Presenter: How does that happen?
Neuren: 1. The IT department just changes printers.
2. No one checks what stock they have OR speaks with the stores manager.
3. They have an expensive SAP system implemented that’s cost us billions that has the stock numbers in it, but apparently no one checks it…

Show: 59.28 – 59.50 [WALKING ALONG SHELVES SEEING DEAD STOCK]
VOICE OF ACTOR: 18:05 Employee: that thing hurts me, I alluded to that last time you were here, I have a problem where, you say to me, your department uses Lexmark 500, (shows hands giving) lexmark 500, how many do you want for a department? you say I want 1000 cartridges 18.23
a thousand uh cartridges I buy a thousand cartridges three months down the line, somebody decides from wherever I sitting to say I'm no longer using Lexmark now I'm using HP, now I've got your stock in storage which is no longer moving, and not just minimum stock, 18.39 I order in bulk, but that things are made on contract so if I order 500 cartridges and you take only 300, 200 gets wasted.

Visual: 52.38 [walk down isle of stock that they no longer can use cos there’s no printers for them]
VO: Row after row of useless stock. [pause] Sometimes IT seemingly changes printer models, other times they change suppliers.

Undercover footage: 42.10 OKI (PRINTER COMPANY), we no longer order OKI, [he opens doors showing all the stock that we no longer order – just wasted left over stock]
Sasha: so do we no longer have OKI as a supplier?
C: have those printers just expire?
Employee: we don't have those printers so nobody's collecting them

VO: It all builds to a grim little punchline.

Councillor: You probably carry more stock than an actual supplier haha

VO: On paper: R104 million in stock. In reality: roughly R40 million can’t be used—either expired or there’s no compatible printer.

Sasha: its 104 million?
Employee: yes on this store alone. they've got four stores, but on this one is hundred million 53.55 and after 100 million maybe 40 million does not work anymore
Sasha: maybe 40 million sho!

Neuren: INtv:80 million?

VO: The Bottom line? Millions converted into cartridges, gathering dust—because the City’s asset control is weak, it’s procurement isn’t standardised, and this mess invites exploitation.

Undercover:
Employee: 35:10 A cartridge, see will see, this one can easily cost R1,200, but here it's R2,800.
Councillor: Double. and that's with profit probably.
Councillor: 1,200 has already got a profit. 30% maybe.
Employee: so others are making 60%, 200%
Councillor: get rich quick?
Employee: on cartridges 35.19
Councillor: that's a big money item

CYAKHULA SECTION:

VO: We finally got our hands on a partial invoice: R2.5 million paid last year to Cyakhula Business Solutions. On paper, they’re only one of the City’s ink suppliers. Their bare-bones website name-drops big-brand “partners”—but when we asked, Canon and Lenovo both told us they’re not partners and didn’t authorise the use of their logos.

Presenter link: And the address? It traces to this boutique hotel in Northcliff—not a warehouse. Rooms are over two thousand rand a night. Ink… with room service?

The company’s directors: Duduzile Simkhumba and Thandiwe Dube may be tenderpreneuers who also direct a Hygiene Service company— clearly complimentary work right?

ROR: Cyakhula business solutions…


(MAYBE WE GET ANOTHER INVOICE)



ACT 3:
We wanted to ask the City about all this… and then remembered: replies are a renewable resource—just not here.
ROR [we’ll include their answers if and when they arrive. I think we need to add in some comedy and come up with a way of approaching them, cos they likely won’t sit down with us.]

VO: Ink isn’t the only waste. Paper is also expensive, even going paperless, council still draws 2–3 pallets of paper from Smit StreeEmployee:80 boxes a pallet, 2,500 sheets a box – more than half a million pages in a single meeting.

Employee: normally the lady, patience (her name) which of you guys know, she comes here and they will take 500 boxes to bring to to print the agenda overnight and deliver to the councillors but now they've reduced it to 500 to 300.
Councillor: per council meeting?
Emloyee: per council meeting yes…

Neuren: and where does that paper go if its not used? We know it never comes back.

VO: And where there’s too much ink, there’s too little of everything else. Toner-rich, pen-poor — the everyday stationary shelves are bare.

UPSOUND: 55:30 Employee: Its mostly empty because there's no contract in place the big boss wants to appoint one person, for 3 years for one item. yeah so we have empty shelves like that
Sasha: so it's just empty because there's no contract currently?
Employee: there's no suppliers, suppliers are withdrawing, supplies are withdrawing, because you cannot give this person [this pins] for three years
Employee: to supply two rands for three years. 55.56 it doesn't make sense cause it doesn't move.

VO: On stationery, Pietersen says the City appointed 36 companies on an “as-and-when” panel—worth up to R45 million. The catch? Low-value items (think a R2 pen) aren’t worth the delivery run. Result: shelves stay empty, even with suppliers on paper.

Neuren intv:
Presenter: Who’s responsible for overseeing the stores?
Neuren: Aubrey Mochela, head of IT. The people on the ground aren’t being consulted on what stock we have or when printers are replaced. That’s reckless and wasteful. He’s pushing the City to act like an IT service provider—which is absurd.

VO: Pietersen says Mochela’s plan includes City-run Wi-Fi hotspots—with the municipality building and owning the infrastructure instead of using service providers.

Neuren: That will cost residents a lot. It risks another white elephant —because private providers already do this. We’re reinventing the wheel for billions.

VO: He’s been in the City for 11 years, and previously served as CIO at City Power. We asked Mr Mochela and the City’s IT department to respond [we’ll include their answers if and when they arrive.]

Neuren intv:
Presenter: Do they know what’s going on?
Neuren: “They do—but they don’t want you to know what’s going on.”
Presenter: So what do we think is happening?
Neuren: “If we can’t find where the ink is going, what are we left to suspect? Is the ink actually getting to a printer in the City of Johannesburg?”
Presenter: And if it isn’t—what does that mean? Are we just… rotating stock?
Neuren: “We don’t know. But as a public representative doing oversight, how can I tell residents we’re getting value for money—legally—if we can’t track it?

VO: If the dead stock isn’t liquidated or auctioned, we’re watching up to millions go down the drain—the kind of money that could build a substation or 200 RDP houses. A City that says it’s broke—while this sits on a shelf.





Further information:
Pitch: Inked Up – Johannesburg City has an Ink Addiction: “A mountain of ink, and a supplier whose address leads not to a warehouse — but to a boutique hotel. In Joburg, nothing adds up.”
Johannesburg likes to say it’s actively pursuing a paperless future. But there’s one small problem: the City is absolutely drowning in ink. Every quarter, the City of Johannesburg splashes out R10 million on printer cartridges. By now, the stockpile at the Smit Street Stores warehouse is worth over R100 million. (And yes — we’ve got the photos to prove it.) The kicker? None of the stock fits printers the City still owns.
So, what’s going on? Councillor Neuren Pietersen has been pressing that question in Council for months. [Video of him council] On an oversight visit a few weeks ago, he took these photos inside Smit Street Stores: pallets stacked to the ceiling, cartridges gathering dust like a hoarder’s paradise. And then outside — the strangest discovery of all.
“The City keeps buying millions of rands’ worth of ink every quarter — and yet, at Smit Street, some of it was found being burned behind the warehouse.”
Yes. Ink. Being burned. [see pictures] No one can explain it. They said much of the ink they order goes to the JMPD. [I’m awaiting to see what they say as I requested answers from them, but the JMPD says they hardly print anything and much of their printing is outsourced.]
And the contradictions run even deeper. This is the same municipality that outsources the printing of much of its own paperwork — as we revealed in our Park Capture investigation, where even tender documents are farmed out. If Joburg isn’t printing its own documents, then what exactly is all this ink for?
Here’s where the story turns. Pietersen has been trying for months to get the requisition documents and invoices. City officials have been cagey. Finally, he was handed one invoice. Just one.
It showed the City had spent R2.5 million on about 400 cartridges. A simple google shows they are seemly overpriced, but I’m waiting for Lexmark South Africa to confirm that. They’ll be coming back to us later this week with final figures — but already the numbers don’t add up. So we dug deeper into the supplier. And that’s when we found it.
An invoice finally revealed the City’s supplier: Cyakhula Business Solutions. On paper, Joburg’s chosen ink dealer. In reality? The company is fronted by two BEE women about whom almost nothing is known online. Their website is extremely basic — the sort of “quickly made” site you’d expect from a start-up side hustle, not a company trusted with multimillion-rand contracts. They also happen to own a hygiene company, which itself has popped up in municipal tenders. And then comes the kicker: Cyakhula’s registered address isn’t a warehouse. It isn’t even an office park. It’s a boutique hotel in Northcliff. Perhaps the ink comes with room service?
Visually, this story plays out like a satire: warehouses stacked with cartridges nobody can use; a glossy hotel doubling as a “supplier.” Pietersen says I can likely join him on an oversight visit — and even capture some undercover footage of the mountains of ink inside Smit Street Stores. And just when viewers think it can’t get any more absurd, the final twist: every councillor is supposed to be entitled to a single cartridge each quarter as part of their tools of trade. Pietersen put in his request. It was denied. One cartridge for a councillor is apparently too much. But a hundred million sitting in a warehouse? That’s perfectly fine. So while we are battling crumbling infrastructure, the city is wasting R10 million every quarter on ink. “If only the City could print working water pipes, electricity, and roads as easily as it prints invoices for ink.”
Councillor Neuren Pietersen has been in office since 2016, and he’s well-known around Johannesburg for trying to hold officials accountable. Always in his trademark fedora, he’s quite a character — the kind of councillor who won’t stop asking awkward questions.

HIGH ON INK

(Masa VO) It was a… slow morning at the City of Johannesburg’s July Council meeting...
Until DA Councillor Neuren Pietersen's passionate report-back from his latest visit to the City’s storerooms…

(Pietersen) We still don’t know why we have R100 million worth of ink cartridges in stock that the City no longer uses!

(Masa VO) Now THAT grabbed our attention! He sends us photos from that oversight visit which shows millions of rands in toner cartridges stuck in a City warehouse - much of it, he says, not being used.

(Pietersen) For a first-class African city, we should be doing better.

(Masa VO) What a waste!

(Masa link) At a time when the City seems to be scrambling for funds to fix potholes and keep the lights on - even going so far as to contemplate selling off public assets like our parks - why is it spending a fortune on ink cartridges that it doesn’t even use? Instead of following the money, in this story, we follow the ink trail…


(Masa VO) When Ward Councillor Pietersen joined the City’s finance committee, he spotted something that didn’t make sense.

(Pietersen) Something stood out for me as to why we were holding so much stock at one of our stores, It was literally 100 million Rand as opposed to 1 to 5 million Rand in the others.

(Masa Link) This warehouse on Smit Street is one of four that the City uses to store consumables for its various departments. That could mean anything from toilet paper to cleaning products. Inside just this building is sitting stock to the value of over R100 million. No, it’s not a hoard of gold: it’s stationery!

(Masa VO) We want to see it for ourselves. So we tag along on another oversight visit with Pietersen — and fellow Councillor David Foley.

(Producer) Okay but those Lexmarks are expired?
(Employee) Yes, these ones are expired. They’re ten years old.
(Producer) Ten years!

(Masa VO) The employees are unaware that we’re filming this guided tour, but it's obvious what fills most of the two story building… floor to ceiling pallets of toner cartridges.

(Pietersen) We are spending on average about 10 million Rand every quarter.
(Masa) R10 million? On stationery?
(Pietersen) On stationery.
(Masa) How much stationery are you using as councillors?
(Pietersen) I have never received a pen from the city of Johannesburg, an eraser or a paper clip even.

(Masa VO) On ink alone, the City has spent a small fortune in the last three years - R126 million! Yet, we couldn’t find one cartridge tender online.

(Pietersen) And this is what we keep on asking. We just get this report saying R10 million spent and then we say 30,000 items were bought, 30,000 what? There's no detail, no breakdown.

(Masa VO) On top of the transparency gap, the City is moving towards a paperless existence. So where are the printers using all this ink?

(Employee) These are ink cartridges mainly used by the JMPD. They actually print your traffic fines, your discs, all registrations, your car registrations ownership... So they consume a lot of cartridges. They take at least 500 a month.

(Masa VO) But according to Pietersen, the Johannesburg Metro Police Department, or JMPD, doesn’t even own all of its printers.

(Pietersen) We investigated why JMPD, what printers are they using? But then on further investigation, that department says they rent their printers as well.
(Masa) So if they rent their printers, wouldn't it come with cartridges?
(Pietersen) Well, I've literally received information that that is what happens.

(Masa VO) So even the heaviest consumer only uses some of the cartridges the City buys - because the rented printers come with regular toner replacements. And the JMPD is not alone: the majority of Joburg’s departments rent printers. The rest, apparently, outsource most printing to contractors.


(Masa Link) But the City continues to buy and store thousands of cartridges that arrive in this warehouse… and many, we’re told, never leave.

(Employee) Take a picture and save it. It may never move again. A million rand stuck standing here.

(Masa VO) Yep, a cool million rand parked on a pallet. Why? The City’s IT department replaced the printer models these cartridges were bought for.

(Pietersen) We are ordering at a time 300, 400 cartridges, and then it turns out that we don't even end that printer anymore.
(Employee) This was the old cartridge that JMPD was using, another million.
(Councillor) And how long has it been standing here?
(Employee) It's almost a year now.

(Masa VO) The City’s central IT department shops for printers - but each department, from the JMPD to Council, is responsible for ordering consumables like cartridges. Everyone is supposed to consult an online inventory system, worth billions, to guide these decisions. But warehouse staff say nobody consults the system - or asks what’s in stock.

(Employee) IT does not consult with me, ‘how many cartridges of this are you having before I change the machine?’ There's no communication.

(Masa VO) You’d think the City would choose a single brand for all its printing supplies - because right now, the warehouse looks more like a brand catalogue.

(Producer) Canon, HP, Brother, OKI, Lexmark.
(Councillor) See, that's why it's so important to standardise, hey.

(Masa VO) What's more, much of the ink has expired.

(Employee) All of those are expired.
(Producer) So those are expired?
(Employee) Yes. These ones are expired. over 10 years old
(Producer) 10 years?
(Employee) Yes R2.7 million worth of expired stock.

(Masa VO) It all builds to a grim punchline.

[Councillor] You probably carry more stock than an actual supplier.

(Employee) Understand that I've got 100 million worth of ink cartridges, but I've got R20 million expired and R20 million of dead stock. So the reality is, take the bosses, bring them here.

(Masa VO) So roughly forty million rands worth of ink stock can’t be used - either it’s expired, or there’s no compatible printer. And there’s no asset register. It’s an asset management disaster.


(Masa Link) We asked the City for answers, but they didn’t sit down with us INSTEAD they sent a lengthy written reply…Ironically, it prints nicely in paper and ink!

(Masa VO) The City responded on behalf of all its departments. It was at pains to explain that the stock worth R108 million at Smit Street is all stationery, not ink alone - but didn’t share numbers. It claims stock doesn’t pile up but moves “immediately”, and says old cartridges are economically stored for 10-15 years because a compatible printer “might” appear.

(Pietersen) Why hold 50 cartridges for one person who may need one ink cartridge?

(Masa VO) Store employees may have the answer.

(Councillor) Why are they so resistant to say, ‘Okay we've made a mistake.’ Write it off, move on?
(Employee) When you know that you have blundered, you will not stand up.

(Masa VO) In other words, no one wants to raise a hand when there’s forty million rand in mistakes! Despite our evidence to the contrary, the City says it does consult existing stock records, the JMPD does use the ink for its leased printers and ink supply tenders are published quarterly.

(Masa) What do you think is really happening here?
(Pietersen) I still have to find these printers that we own. That's the big mystery.
(Masa) We don't know where the ink is going.
(Pietersen) Indeed. If we can't manage something as simple as ink cartridges, how on earth are we managing the rest of the city?

(Masa VO) The City says auctions don’t fetch much. But surely, if stock isn’t used, sold, or written off, it just bleeds value— In a cash-strapped city, why let a small fortune sit on a shelf?

We have really great footage, and have a compelling story that will illustrate what a mess the asset management system is. In short: it says Joburg talks “modern, paperless city,” but runs on procure-first, plan-later. Transparency gap: basic spend and contracts aren’t clearly published or explained. Control failure: stock counts, write-offs, and auctions aren’t working; SAP/asset data isn’t driving decisions. No standardisation: departments/IT change printers without checking stores → waste by design. Misaligned incentives: outsourced printing + leased printers (toner included) while buying separate cartridges anyway. Service impact: money that should fix pipes, power and roads is frozen on shelves. Accountability vacuum: everyone’s “aware,” nobody owns it. Bottom line: not just wastage—a governance problem that bleeds budgets and trust. Result: shelves stay empty, even with suppliers on paper. Neuren intv: Presenter: Who’s responsible for overseeing the stores? Neuren: Aubrey Mochela, head of IT. The people on the ground aren’t being consulted on what stock we have or when printers are replaced. That’s reckless and wasteful. He’s pushing the City to act like an IT service provider—which is absurd. VO: Pietersen says Mochela’s plan includes City-run Wi-Fi hotspots—with the municipality building and owning the infrastructure instead of using service providers. Neuren: That will cost residents a lot. It risks another white elephant —because private providers already do this. We’re reinventing the wheel for billions. VO: He’s been in the City for 11 years, and previously served as CIO at City Power. VO: If the dead stock isn’t liquidated or auctioned, we’re watching up to millions go down the drain—the kind of money that could build a substation or 200 RDP houses. A City that says it’s broke—while this sits on a shelf. Further information: Pitch: Inked Up – Johannesburg City has an Ink Addiction: “A mountain of ink, and a supplier whose address leads not to a warehouse — but to a boutique hotel. In Joburg, nothing adds up.” Johannesburg likes to say it’s actively pursuing a paperless future. But there’s one small problem: the City is absolutely drowning in ink. Every quarter, the City of Johannesburg splashes out R10 million on printer cartridges. By now, the stockpile at the Smit Street Stores warehouse is worth over R100 million. (And yes — we’ve got the photos to prove it.) The kicker? None of the stock fits printers the City still owns. So, what’s going on? Councillor Neuren Pietersen has been pressing that question in Council for months. [Video of him council] On an oversight visit a few weeks ago, he took these photos inside Smit Street Stores: pallets stacked to the ceiling, cartridges gathering dust like a hoarder’s paradise. And then outside — the strangest discovery of all. “The City keeps buying millions of rands’ worth of ink every quarter — and yet, at Smit Street, some of it was found being burned behind the warehouse.” Yes. Ink. Being burned. [see pictures] No one can explain it. They said much of the ink they order goes to the JMPD. [I’m awaiting to see what they say as I requested answers from them, but the JMPD says they hardly print anything and much of their printing is outsourced.] And the contradictions run even deeper. This is the same municipality that outsources the printing of much of its own paperwork — as we revealed in our Park Capture investigation, where even tender documents are farmed out. If Joburg isn’t printing its own documents, then what exactly is all this ink for? Here’s where the story turns. Pietersen has been trying for months to get the requisition documents and invoices. City officials have been cagey. Finally, he was handed one invoice. Just one. It showed the City had spent R2.5 million on about 400 cartridges. A simple google shows they are seemly overpriced, but I’m waiting for Lexmark South Africa to confirm that. They’ll be coming back to us later this week with final figures — but already the numbers don’t add up. So we dug deeper into the supplier. And that’s when we found it. An invoice finally revealed the City’s supplier: Cyakhula Business Solutions. On paper, Joburg’s chosen ink dealer. In reality? The company is fronted by two BEE women about whom almost nothing is known online. Their website is extremely basic — the sort of “quickly made” site you’d expect from a start-up side hustle, not a company trusted with multimillion-rand contracts. They also happen to own a hygiene company, which itself has popped up in municipal tenders. And then comes the kicker: Cyakhula’s registered address isn’t a warehouse. It isn’t even an office park. It’s a boutique hotel in Northcliff. Perhaps the ink comes with room service? Visually, this story plays out like a satire: warehouses stacked with cartridges nobody can use; a glossy hotel doubling as a “supplier.” Pietersen says I can likely join him on an oversight visit — and even capture some undercover footage of the mountains of ink inside Smit Street Stores. And just when viewers think it can’t get any more absurd, the final twist: every councillor is supposed to be entitled to a single cartridge each quarter as part of their tools of trade. Pietersen put in his request. It was denied. One cartridge for a councillor is apparently too much. But a hundred million sitting in a warehouse? That’s perfectly fine. So while we are battling crumbling infrastructure, the city is wasting R10 million every quarter on ink. “If only the City could print working water pipes, electricity, and roads as easily as it prints invoices for ink.” Councillor Neuren Pietersen has been in office since 2016, and he’s well-known around Johannesburg for trying to hold officials accountable. Always in his trademark fedora, he’s quite a character — the kind of councillor who won’t stop asking awkward questions. He sends us photos from that oversight visit which shows millions of rands in toner cartridges stuck in a City warehouse - much of it, he says, not being used. (Pietersen) For a first-class African city, we should be doing better. (Masa VO) What a waste! (Pietersen) Something stood out for me as to why we were holding so much stock at one of our stores, It was literally 100 million Rand as opposed to 1 to 5 million Rand in the others. Inside just this building is sitting stock to the value of over R100 million. No, it’s not a hoard of gold: it’s stationery! (Masa VO) We want to see it for ourselves. So we tag along on another oversight visit with Pietersen — and fellow Councillor David Foley. (Producer) Okay but those Lexmarks are expired? (Employee) Yes, these ones are expired. They’re ten years old. (Producer) Ten years! (Masa VO) The employees are unaware that we’re filming this guided tour, but it's obvious what fills most of the two story building… floor to ceiling pallets of toner cartridges. (Pietersen) We are spending on average about 10 million Rand every quarter. (Masa) R10 million? On stationery? (Pietersen) On stationery. (Masa) How much stationery are you using as councillors? (Pietersen) I have never received a pen from the city of Johannesburg, an eraser or a paper clip even. (Masa VO) On ink alone, the City has spent a small fortune in the last three years - R126 million! Yet, we couldn’t find one cartridge tender online. (Pietersen) And this is what we keep on asking. We just get this report saying R10 million spent and then we say 30,000 items were bought, 30,000 what? There's no detail, no breakdown. (Masa VO) On top of the transparency gap, the City is moving towards a paperless existence. So where are the printers using all this ink? (Employee) These are ink cartridges mainly used by the JMPD. They actually print your traffic fines, your discs, all registrations, your car registrations ownership... So they consume a lot of cartridges. They take at least 500 a month. (Masa VO) But according to Pietersen, the Johannesburg Metro Police Department, or JMPD, doesn’t even own all of its printers. (Pietersen) We investigated why JMPD, what printers are they using? But then on further investigation, that department says they rent their printers as well. (Masa) So if they rent their printers, wouldn't it come with cartridges? (Pietersen) Well, I've literally received information that that is what happens. (Masa VO) So even the heaviest consumer only uses some of the cartridges the City buys - because the rented printers come with regular toner replacements. And the JMPD is not alone: the majority of Joburg’s departments rent printers. The rest, apparently, outsource most printing to contractors. (Masa Link) But the City continues to buy and store thousands of cartridges that arrive in this warehouse… and many, we’re told, never leave. (Employee) Take a picture and save it. It may never move again. A million rand stuck standing here. (Masa VO) Yep, a cool million rand parked on a pallet. Why? The City’s IT department replaced the printer models these cartridges were bought for. (Pietersen) We are ordering at a time 300, 400 cartridges, and then it turns out that we don't even end that printer anymore. (Employee) This was the old cartridge that JMPD was using, another million. (Councillor) And how long has it been standing here? (Employee) It's almost a year now. (Masa VO) The City’s central IT department shops for printers - but each department, from the JMPD to Council, is responsible for ordering consumables like cartridges. Everyone is supposed to consult an online inventory system, worth billions, to guide these decisions. But warehouse staff say nobody consults the system - or asks what’s in stock. (Employee) IT does not consult with me, ‘how many cartridges of this are you having before I change the machine?’ There's no communication. (Masa VO) You’d think the City would choose a single brand for all its printing supplies - because right now, the warehouse looks more like a brand catalogue. (Producer) Canon, HP, Brother, OKI, Lexmark. (Councillor) See, that's why it's so important to standardise, hey. (Masa VO) What's more, much of the ink has expired. (Employee) All of those are expired. (Producer) So those are expired? (Employee) Yes. These ones are expired. over 10 years old (Producer) 10 years? (Employee) Yes R2.7 million worth of expired stock. (Masa VO) It all builds to a grim punchline. [Councillor] You probably carry more stock than an actual supplier. (Employee) Understand that I've got 100 million worth of ink cartridges, but I've got R20 million expired and R20 million of dead stock. So the reality is, take the bosses, bring them here. (Masa VO) So roughly forty million rands worth of ink stock can’t be used - either it’s expired, or there’s no compatible printer. And there’s no asset register. It’s an asset management disaster. (Masa Link) We asked the City for answers, but they didn’t sit down with us INSTEAD they sent a lengthy written reply…Ironically, it prints nicely in paper and ink! (Masa VO) The City responded on behalf of all its departments. It was at pains to explain that the stock worth R108 million at Smit Street is all stationery, not ink alone - but didn’t share numbers. It claims stock doesn’t pile up but moves “immediately”, and says old cartridges are economically stored for 10-15 years because a compatible printer “might” appear. (Pietersen) Why hold 50 cartridges for one person who may need one ink cartridge? (Masa VO) Store employees may have the answer. (Councillor) Why are they so resistant to say, ‘Okay we've made a mistake.’ Write it off, move on? (Employee) When you know that you have blundered, you will not stand up. (Masa VO) In other words, no one wants to raise a hand when there’s forty million rand in mistakes! Despite our evidence to the contrary, the City says it does consult existing stock records, the JMPD does use the ink for its leased printers and ink supply tenders are published quarterly. (Masa) What do you think is really happening here? (Pietersen) I still have to find these printers that we own. That's the big mystery. (Masa) We don't know where the ink is going. (Pietersen) Indeed. If we can't manage something as simple as ink cartridges, how on earth are we managing the rest of the city? (Masa VO) The City says auctions don’t fetch much. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A “paperless” Joburg is hoarding over R100 million in ink, R40 million of which can’t be used —exposing chaotic procurement, mountains of dead stock, and a supplier address that leads to a bou
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We went undercover to the smit street stores to see the chaos. We have really great footage, and have a compelling story that will illustrate what a mess the asset management system is. In short: it says Joburg talks “modern, paperless city,” but runs on procure-first, plan-later. Transparency gap: basic spend and contracts aren’t clearly published or explained. Control failure: stock counts, write-offs, and auctions aren’t working; SAP/asset data isn’t driving decisions. No standardisation: departments/IT change printers without checking stores → waste by design. Misaligned incentives: outsourced printing + leased printers (toner included) while buying separate cartridges anyway. Service impact: money that should fix pipes, power and roads is frozen on shelves. Accountability vacuum: everyone’s “aware,” nobody owns it. Bottom line: not just wastage—a governance problem that bleeds budgets and trust.

metadata.Further information: Pitch: Inked Up – Johannesburg City has an Ink Addiction: “A mountain of ink, and a supplier whose address leads not to a warehouse — but to a boutique hotel. In Joburg, nothing adds up.” Johannesburg likes to say it’s actively pursuing a paperless future. But there’s one small problem: the City is absolutely drowning in ink. Every quarter, the City of Johannesburg splashes out R10 million on printer cartridges. By now, the stockpile at the Smit Street Stores warehouse is worth over R100 million. (And yes — we’ve got the photos to prove it.) The kicker? None of the stock fits printers the City still owns. So, what’s going on? Councillor Neuren Pietersen has been pressing that question in Council for months. [Video of him council] On an oversight visit a few weeks ago, he took these photos inside Smit Street Stores: pallets stacked to the ceiling, cartridges gathering dust like a hoarder’s paradise. And then outside — the strangest discovery of all. “The City keeps buying millions of rands’ worth of ink every quarter — and yet, at Smit Street, some of it was found being burned behind the warehouse.” Yes. Ink. Being burned. [see pictures] No one can explain it. They said much of the ink they order goes to the JMPD. [I’m awaiting to see what they say as I requested answers from them, but the JMPD says they hardly print anything and much of their printing is outsourced.] And the contradictions run even deeper. This is the same municipality that outsources the printing of much of its own paperwork — as we revealed in our Park Capture investigation, where even tender documents are farmed out. If Joburg isn’t printing its own documents, then what exactly is all this ink for? Here’s where the story turns. Pietersen has been trying for months to get the requisition documents and invoices. City officials have been cagey. Finally, he was handed one invoice. Just one. It showed the City had spent R2.5 million on about 400 cartridges. A simple google shows they are seemly overpriced, but I’m waiting for Lexmark South Africa to confirm that. They’ll be coming back to us later this week with final figures — but already the numbers don’t add up. So we dug deeper into the supplier. And that’s when we found it. An invoice finally revealed the City’s supplier: Cyakhula Business Solutions. On paper, Joburg’s chosen ink dealer. In reality? The company is fronted by two BEE women about whom almost nothing is known online. Their website is extremely basic — the sort of “quickly made” site you’d expect from a start-up side hustle, not a company trusted with multimillion-rand contracts. They also happen to own a hygiene company, which itself has popped up in municipal tenders. And then comes the kicker: Cyakhula’s registered address isn’t a warehouse. It isn’t even an office park. It’s a boutique hotel in Northcliff. Perhaps the ink comes with room service? Visually, this story plays out like a satire: warehouses stacked with cartridges nobody can use; a glossy hotel doubling as a “supplier.” Pietersen says I can likely join him on an oversight visit — and even capture some undercover footage of the mountains of ink inside Smit Street Stores. And just when viewers think it can’t get any more absurd, the final twist: every councillor is supposed to be entitled to a single cartridge each quarter as part of their tools of trade. Pietersen put in his request. It was denied. One cartridge for a councillor is apparently too much. But a hundred million sitting in a warehouse? That’s perfectly fine. So while we are battling crumbling infrastructure, the city is wasting R10 million every quarter on ink. “If only the City could print working water pipes, electricity, and roads as easily as it prints invoices for ink.” Councillor Neuren Pietersen has been in office since 2016, and he’s well-known around Johannesburg for trying to hold officials accountable. Always in his trademark fedora, he’s quite a character — the kind of councillor who won’t stop asking awkward questions.
